query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multiscale simulation approach that couples DFT-based phonon dispersion calculations with machine learning-enhanced atomistic models to separately quantify lattice and electronic heat transport will predict the thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr with an improved accuracy (±20% error margin) compared to earlier methods (±50%), when evaluated at both low and high temperature ranges.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr in its near-pristine crystalline state and a variant with 1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Apply a combined DFT and ML-based potential simulation that first uses ab initio phonon calculations (bypassing the Debye approximation) for defect‐free or near‐pristine configurations at low temperatures (50–300 K) and then uses atomistic simulations with Monte Carlo sampling to incorporate realistic defects (e.g., vacancies, interstitials, 1 wt.% oxygen) at elevated temperatures (300–1200 K).
generation.conditions: The approach is valid for simulated and experimental configurations over the temperature range 50–1200 K, with separate evaluations in the sub-200 K region (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) and in the 300–1200 K range (on samples with realistic defect/impurity levels).
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale lattice structure—including defect distributions and impurity incorporation—mediates the separation of phonon scattering processes from electron scattering mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: The method disentangles heat transport contributors by directly calculating phonon dispersion curves and simulating independent electron scattering events, thus avoiding oversimplifications like the Debye temperature approximation and the ideal defect‐free assumption. This separation leads to more accurate thermal conductivity estimates by accounting for the full atomic-scale complexity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new approach will yield independent estimates for lattice and electronic thermal conductivities that, when combined, predict total thermal conductivity values within ±20% of experimental measurements (e.g., ~10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures for oxygen-doped samples), significantly reducing the predictive error relative to earlier approximations.
generation.baseline: Earlier predictive methods typically used Debye temperature approximations or perfect bulk crystal simulations that conflated lattice and electronic contributions and exhibited error margins of around ±50%.
generation.boundary: The predictions are expected to be reliable for temperatures between 50 K and 1200 K and for samples that are either nearly defect-free or contain realistic impurity levels (1 wt.% oxygen). Beyond this temperature range or with extreme microstructural disorder, the approach may not capture additional complexities such as phase instabilities.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the quantitative contribution of electron scattering at very low temperatures (<200 K) where experimental separation is challenging, and the exact effect of heterogeneous defect distributions on the high-temperature regime.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct complementary experimental measurements that independently quantify lattice (phonon) and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr samples. This includes measurements on pristine samples in the 50–300 K range and on oxygen-doped samples (1 wt.%) in the 300–1200 K range. Compare these with the simulation predictions for both separate contributions and the total thermal conductivity.
measurements: Direct measurement of total thermal conductivity using steady-state or transient methods across the designated temperature ranges.
Independent separation of lattice and electronic contributions using techniques such as low-temperature thermal Hall measurements or modulation methods.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined predicted thermal conductivity deviates by more than ±20% from the experimental value, or if the separately predicted lattice and electronic contributions do not match their independently measured counterparts, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
